subject: Computer Networking
title: The Three-Way Handshake
description: A quick, practical guide to The Three-Way Handshake.

hook.text: Before two computers share a single byte, they perform a three-step introduction.

buildup.text: Step one: the client sends SYN — 'I want to connect.' Step two: the server replies SYN-ACK — 'Got it, ready.'

discovery.text: Step three: the client confirms with ACK. Now both sides know the connection is alive and mutual.

twist.text: Without this handshake, a server could waste resources on connections that never complete.

climax.text: SYN floods exploit this — sending fake SYNs to overwhelm a server. That's a denial-of-service attack.

punchline.text: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Three steps to trust.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of a TCP three-way handshake?

details.summary: TCP establishes connections through a three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with ACK. This exchange synchronizes sequence numbers and confirms both sides are ready to communicate before any data is sent.
details.whyItMatters: Every TCP connection starts with this handshake. It adds one round trip of latency to every new connection, which is why connection reuse and HTTP/2 matter for performance.
takeaways: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK is the three-step connection establishment
The handshake synchronizes sequence numbers between endpoints
It adds one round-trip time of latency to new connections

faq.question: Why does TCP need a three-way handshake instead of just two steps?
faq.answer: Two messages would only confirm one direction works. The third message confirms the server's response reached the client, verifying both directions can communicate. It also prevents old duplicate connection requests from accidentally opening unwanted connections.

faq.question: How do SYN flood attacks exploit the handshake?
faq.answer: Attackers send thousands of SYN packets without completing the handshake. The server allocates memory for each half-open connection, exhausting resources. SYN cookies defend against this by encoding connection state in the SYN-ACK response, avoiding memory allocation until the handshake completes.
